stem: The student wants to provide an example of a mutually beneficial relationship between two species. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Mutualism is a relationship between two species in which both species benefit.
• Mutualistic relationships are common among species that live on coral reefs.
• The bluestreak cleaner wrasse is a small reef fish that removes parasites from the bodies of larger reef fish.
• The wrasse gets a meal of parasites, and the larger fish is rid of pests that could harm it.
• Many reef fish visit the wrasse's "cleaning stations" several times a day.
choices: Mutualism, in which two species both benefit, is a type of relationship common among the species living on coral reefs.
The bluestreak cleaner wrasse and the larger reef fish it cleans benefit each other: the wrasse gets a meal, and the larger fish loses its parasites.
Larger reef fish benefit from the bluestreak cleaner wrasse, which gains nothing for itself by removing their parasites.
The bluestreak cleaner wrasse, a small reef fish, removes parasites from the larger fish that visit its cleaning stations.
explanation: The goal asks for an example, so you need one named pair of species, and you need to show that the relationship is mutually beneficial. The notes call this 'mutualism'. Choice B names the bluestreak cleaner wrasse and the larger fish it cleans, and it states what each one gains. That makes it a specific instance of the property the goal names.

A.why: You chose the category-level definition. This choice describes mutualism in general and names no particular species, so it makes a generalization instead of giving an example.

C.why: You may have chosen this because it names a specific species. However, it says the wrasse gains nothing, and the notes say the wrasse gets a meal. A relationship that benefits only one side is not mutually beneficial.

D.why: This choice names a specific instance, but it shows only one side of the benefit: the larger fish lose their parasites. It never says what the wrasse gains, so it doesn't show that the relationship is mutually beneficial.

• Along New Zealand's Hikurangi margin, shallow slow slip events recur about every 18 to 24 months.

choices: Along the Cascadia subduction zone in the Pacific Northwest, slow slip events have recurred roughly every 14 months.
Slow slip events recur about every 14 months in Cascadia, whereas they recur every 18 to 24 months along the Hikurangi margin.
Slow slip events unfold over days to months, releasing stress gradually and generally without shaking that people can feel.
Slow slip events are reliably followed by larger earthquakes, so seismologists treat them as warnings of coming shaking.
explanation: A generalization makes a claim about the whole category, and no single location or event is its subject. Choice C makes 'slow slip events' as a group its subject and states what is true of them in general: how long they last and how they release stress.

A.why: You picked the wrong level. This choice describes slow slip events in one specific place, Cascadia, so it gives an example instead of a generalization about the category.

B.why: This is the wrong level again. Comparing two specific locations is not a generalization. The relation word 'whereas' makes it a strong comparison, but the goal didn't ask for one.

D.why: The notes say only that researchers are studying whether slow slip events *might* raise the likelihood of larger earthquakes. Saying they are 'reliably followed' by earthquakes claims far more than the notes support.

stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Red dwarfs are the most common type of star in the Milky Way galaxy.
• Most red dwarfs have between 8% and 50% of the Sun's mass.
• Because they burn their hydrogen fuel slowly, red dwarfs are expected to shine for trillions of years.
• The Sun is expected to shine for roughly 10 billion years in total.
• Proxima Centauri, a red dwarf, is the nearest star to the Sun and is expected to shine for about 4 trillion years.
choices: Proxima Centauri, a red dwarf, is expected to shine for about 4 trillion years, far longer than the Sun's lifespan of roughly 10 billion years.
Red dwarfs are expected to shine for trillions of years, far outlasting the Sun, whose total lifespan is roughly 10 billion years.
Red dwarfs, which have between 8% and 50% of the Sun's mass, are the most common type of star in the Milky Way galaxy.
Red dwarfs are expected to shine for trillions of years, so every other star in the Milky Way will outlast the Sun.
explanation: The goal asks for a generalization, meaning a claim about red dwarfs as a whole category, and it asks you to compare their lifespans with the Sun's. Choice B uses the plural category noun 'red dwarfs' and states the gap directly: trillions of years compared with the Sun's roughly 10 billion. No single star is the subject.

A.why: You picked the wrong level. This choice does compare a lifespan with the Sun's, but its subject is one star, Proxima Centauri. That makes it a specific example, and the goal asked for a generalization about red dwarfs as a group.

C.why: This is a claim about the whole category, but it is about mass and how common red dwarfs are, not about how long they live. You matched the level of the goal but missed its content.

D.why: The notes only cover red dwarfs. This choice extends the claim to 'every other star in the Milky Way,' which the notes never support.

stem: The student wants to present a specific example of a hazard pay premium, including the size of that premium. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Economists use the term "compensating differential" for the extra pay that workers receive for taking jobs with risky or unpleasant conditions.
• Such differentials have been documented in many dangerous occupations.
• Offshore wind technicians repair turbines at height over open water, often in high winds.
• In one regional survey, offshore wind technicians earned a median of $41 per hour.
• Onshore electricians with similar training earned a median of $33 per hour in the same survey.
choices: In one regional survey, offshore wind technicians, who repair turbines at height over open water, earned a median of $41 per hour.
Economists have documented compensating differentials, or extra pay for risky or unpleasant conditions, in many dangerous occupations.
In one regional survey, offshore wind technicians earned $8 more per hour than electricians, showing that all risky jobs pay more.
In one regional survey, offshore wind technicians, who work at height over open water, earned $8 more per hour than similar onshore electricians.
explanation: The goal uses 'hazard pay premium,' which is the notes' 'compensating differential' under another name. It wants one specific instance and the size of the premium. Choice D names a specific occupation, ties it to the hazard (working at height over open water), and gives the gap: $41 − $33 = $8 more per hour than similarly trained onshore electricians.

A.why: This names the right occupation and the hazard, but it gives only one of the two wages. A premium is the difference between the two wages, and $41 on its own doesn't tell you how much extra the technicians earn.

B.why: This is the wrong-level trap. It defines the category and says differentials exist in many occupations, but it never names a specific job or gives a size. The goal asked for an example, not a generalization.

C.why: The $8 gap is correct, but this choice treats one survey of one occupation as proof that 'all risky jobs pay more.' It also drops 'similar onshore,' so it no longer says who the technicians were compared with.

stem: The student wants to make a generalization about the audiences of cumulative tales. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Folklorists classify traditional stories by tale type, a recurring plot pattern.
• In a cumulative tale, each new episode repeats all earlier episodes and adds one new element.
• Folklorist Ines Varga examined 300 recorded tellings of cumulative tales.
• In 225 of the tellings the audience was children; in 75 it was adults.
• One recorded telling of "The Old Woman and Her Pig," an English cumulative tale told to children, ran to 14 episodes.
choices: Cumulative tales are told to children far more often than to adults; in one sample, children were the audience three times as often.
One telling of "The Old Woman and Her Pig," an English cumulative tale told to children, ran to fourteen separate episodes.
Cumulative tales are told to adults far more often than to children; in one sample, adults were the audience three times as often.
Cumulative tales are a tale type in which each new episode repeats all of the earlier episodes and then adds one new element.
explanation: The goal asks for a claim about cumulative tales as a category, specifically about who they are told to. Choice A makes that broad claim and states the gap from Varga's sample: 225 tellings to children against 75 to adults, so children were the audience three times as often.

B.why: This is the wrong-level trap. It mentions an audience of children, but its subject is one telling of one tale. That is a specific example, so it can't stand for cumulative tales as a whole.

C.why: The comparison runs the wrong way. The notes give 225 tellings to children and 75 to adults, so children, not adults, were the audience three times as often.

D.why: This is a real generalization about the category, but it describes how cumulative tales are structured, not who hears them. It is at the right level but answers a different question.
